explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Ananias, the high priest, came down with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus. Tertullus is the one who presented their case against Paul to the governor. A lawyer doing the talking makes sense to me, like the person at the counter who actually knows how to fill out the form.

Gamaliel was a Pharisee and a teacher of the law, respected by all the people (Acts 5:34). He's a real name from Acts, but he isn't in this courtroom. The text says the one who presented the case was a lawyer named Tertullus.

A centurion named Julius does show up in Paul's story, in Acts 27:1. He isn't the one speaking here, though. Ananias and the elders bring a lawyer named Tertullus to present their case to Felix. Julius is a soldier, and this job needed someone with a lot of words.

explanations.answer: Felix brought this nation lasting peace
explanations.explanation: That's it. Tertullus says, “Because of you, we have enjoyed a lasting peace, and your foresight has brought improvements to this nation.” He's talking about the judge before he says a word about the prisoner. I think it sounds like a five-star review from somebody who's about to ask for a refund.

explanations.answer: Felix has kept them waiting too long
explanations.explanation: No complaints about the schedule here. Tertullus opens with praise for Felix, saying the nation has enjoyed a lasting peace because of him. The only thing he says about delay is that he doesn't want to delay Felix any further. He's being very polite before the charges start.

explanations.answer: Felix should send Paul to Rome
explanations.explanation: Rome never comes up in Tertullus's speech. He opens by praising Felix for a lasting peace and improvements to the nation. At the end he tells Felix that by examining Paul himself, he'll learn the truth about their charges (Acts 24:8). So he's asking for an examination, not a trip.

Right, baker. Tertullus calls Paul “…a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes…” That means the one out front, the one everybody is supposedly following. It's a big claim to make about a man standing there under guard.
Tertullus never says deserter. He says Paul is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. Deserter would mean Paul walked away from something. Ringleader means he's out front leading it.

A spy would be sneaking around in the back. Tertullus says the opposite. He calls Paul a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, which is the guy out front. Nobody in this courtroom is accusing him of being quiet.
That's the word. Tertullus says Paul even tried to desecrate the temple, “so we seized him.” That's the accusers' side of the story. Paul is about to give his own.
Released isn't the word. Tertullus says Paul even tried to desecrate the temple, so they seized him. Paul has been called in, and this is the accusers' account of it.
Warned is a lot friendlier than what Tertullus says. He says Paul even tried to desecrate the temple, so they seized him. Seized is the word he uses.
True. Verse 9 says the Jews concurred, asserting that these charges were true. So Tertullus isn't speaking alone. The people with him join in and say the charges are true.
The text says the other way. Acts 24:9 says, “The Jews concurred, asserting that these charges were true.” So the people with Tertullus back him up. They don't stay silent.

Gladly! Paul says, “Knowing that you have been a judge over this nation for many years, I gladly make my defense.” He's standing in front of a governor with the high priest and a lawyer against him, and he says gladly. I'd have been sweating through my apron.

Paul doesn't say nervously. He says he gladly makes his defense, because Felix has been a judge over this nation for many years. Maybe his knees were shaking. The text doesn't say so, and neither will I. What it gives us is gladly.

Angrily isn't the word the text uses. Paul begins, “Knowing that you have been a judge over this nation for many years, I gladly make my defense.” He starts with Felix's many years as a judge. Gladly is the word the text gives.
Right. Paul says it was no more than twelve days ago that he went up to Jerusalem to worship. He tells Felix he can verify it for himself. I bet he's glad the dates can be checked.
Trade is not what Paul says. He went up to Jerusalem to worship, and he says it was no more than twelve days ago. He even tells Felix he can verify it.

No protest here. Paul says he went up to Jerusalem to worship. Right after that he says his accusers did not find him debating with anyone in the temple or riling up a crowd in the synagogues or in the city.

This one says the opposite of what Paul says. In Acts 24:12 he tells Felix, “Yet my accusers did not find me debating with anyone in the temple or riling up a crowd in the synagogues or in the city.” So his answer to the accusation is no, and he doesn't hedge.

False is right. Paul says his accusers did not find him debating with anyone in the temple or riling up a crowd in the synagogues or in the city. He's answering Tertullus point by point. And he adds that they can't prove any of their charges.

explanations.answer: He worships God according to the Way
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Paul says, “I do confess to you, however, that I worship the God of our fathers according to the Way, which they call a sect.” It isn't a crime he's confessing. It's the center of his life. I think that's a pretty bold thing to admit with the accusers sitting right there.

explanations.answer: He brought a Greek into the temple
explanations.explanation: That accusation did come up earlier, when Jews from the province of Asia cried out that Paul had brought Greeks into the temple (Acts 21:27-28). But it's not what Paul confesses here. He confesses that he worships the God of our fathers according to the Way. Nothing about a Greek in this speech.

explanations.answer: He speaks against the Law of Moses
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite. He tells Felix, “I believe everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets…” What he confesses is that he worships the God of our fathers according to the Way. He's not against the Law.

explanations.answer: The righteous and the wicked will rise again
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says he has the same hope in God that his accusers cherish, “…that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.” Both groups, not just one. That's a hope he says he shares with the very men accusing him.

explanations.answer: Only the righteous will rise again
explanations.explanation: Close, but Paul says more. He says there will be “…a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.” Both groups rise. That's the hope he says he shares with his accusers.

explanations.answer: Their names will live on forever
explanations.explanation: Paul isn't talking about a legacy. He says the hope is “…that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.” That means people actually rising, not just being remembered. No plaque, no street named after anybody.

explanations.answer: To bring alms and present offerings
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says. After several years, he returned to Jerusalem “…to bring alms to my people and to present offerings.” That's the reason he gives Felix for the trip.

explanations.answer: To answer charges before the Sanhedrin
explanations.explanation: The Sanhedrin does come up in Paul's speech, but as a place he stood, not as his reason for coming. He says he returned to Jerusalem to bring alms to his people and to present offerings. That's the reason he gives for coming back.

explanations.answer: To confront the men who opposed him
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say he came back for a confrontation. He says he returned to Jerusalem to bring alms to his people and to present offerings. That's the reason he gives for the trip.

True, baker. Paul says, “At the time they found me in the temple, I was ceremonially clean and was not inciting a crowd or an uproar.” He's answering the charge that he tried to desecrate the temple (Acts 24:6). Clean, calm and no uproar is how he describes himself that day.

The text says otherwise. Paul tells Felix that when they found him in the temple, he “…was ceremonially clean and was not inciting a crowd or an uproar.” That's how he answers the charge about the temple. So True is the answer, and this one isn't it.

Not quite. The line Paul says he called out wasn't about the Law of Moses. He says it was this: “It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.” So the one thing he mentions is the resurrection of the dead.

False, and nicely spotted. Paul says the one thing he called out before the Sanhedrin was, “It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.” Nothing in his words there mentions the Law of Moses. The thing he names is the resurrection.

Yes, friends. Felix orders the centurion to keep Paul under guard, but to allow him some freedom and permit his friends to minister to his needs. So Paul is under guard, and his friends are still allowed to help him. I'd take that over the back of the junk drawer I spent years stuck in.

Soldiers isn't the word in the text. Felix orders the centurion to keep Paul under guard, but to allow him some freedom and permit his friends to minister to his needs. The text names Paul's friends as the ones who minister to his needs.

The text doesn't mention servants. Felix orders Paul kept under guard, but with some freedom, and he permits Paul's friends to minister to his needs. Guard and freedom, both in the same order from Felix.

Frightened, baker. As Paul expounded on righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened. Paul wasn't just reading out a to-do list. Whatever else was going on in that room, Felix heard it and it shook him.

The text doesn't say furious. It says that as Paul spoke about righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened. Then he said, “You may go for now. When I find the time, I will call for you.” Frightened is the word the text gives.
Convinced isn't the word the text gives. It says Felix became frightened and said, “You may go for now. When I find the time, I will call for you.” Frightened is what the text tells us.

That's what the text says. Felix was hoping Paul would offer him a bribe, so he sent for Paul frequently and talked with him. I think that explains why the visits kept coming. It's still a hard thing to read about a man who just heard about righteousness.
A blessing isn't what Felix is waiting for. The text says he was hoping Paul would offer him a bribe. That's why he sent for Paul frequently and talked with him.
Verse 26 says Felix was hoping Paul would offer him a bribe. A confession isn't what the text names. The bribe is the hope it gives, and it says he sent for Paul frequently and talked with him.

Yes. The text says, “…wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.” Two years had passed and Festus was taking over, and Paul was still sitting there. I think this is a heavy part of the story, and it's good that it isn't over.
Felix doesn't set Paul free. The text says that wishing to do the Jews a favor, he left Paul in prison. And that's on his way out the door, after two years.
Rome isn't what Felix does here. Acts 24:27 says that, wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison. Then Porcius Festus took his place as governor. Paul stays right where he is.
